meta.title: Merchant Cash Advance Calculator: Worked Comparison
meta.heading: Merchant Cash Advance Calculator: Worked Comparison
meta.description: A factor rate of 1.30 on a $50,000 advance means $65,000 of contracted remittances
meta.cardIntro: A factor rate of 1.30 on a $50,000 advance means $65,000 of contracted remittances. With a $1,500 withheld fee, the business receives $48,500 and pays $16,500 more than that net funding. Annualized cost also depends on the actual remittance dates.

merchant-cash-advance.intro: Separate the factor markup from net cash received. Use a fixed remittance count or a constant-sales holdback scenario, then inspect the dated cash flows and an illustrative effective annual IRR rather than treating the factor as an APR.
merchant-cash-advance.answer: A factor rate of 1.30 on a $50,000 advance means $65,000 of contracted remittances. With a $1,500 withheld fee, the business receives $48,500 and pays $16,500 more than that net funding. Annualized cost also depends on the actual remittance dates.
merchant-cash-advance.exampleNote: Original illustrations checked against independent 70-digit Decimal dated cash-flow and IRA-basis arithmetic. No competitor parity, professional certification or actual lender approval is claimed.

sections.title: What does the factor rate mean?
paragraphs: Multiply the 50,000 gross advance by 1.30 to obtain 65,000 in contracted remittances. The factor markup is 15,000. The factor does not describe when the remittances occur.
A 1,500 fee withheld at funding reduces cash received to 48,500. Total remittances minus that net receipt is 16,500, so the withheld fee is counted once in total cash cost.
sections.formula: Total remittances = advance × factor. Net funding = advance − withheld fees. Effective annual r solves net funding = Σ remittance / (1+r)^(calendar days/365).

sections.title: Why do dates change the annualized cost?
paragraphs: Fixed-count mode places each remittance on your explicit calendar after the entered first date. Weekday mode skips weekends only; no public-holiday calendar or assumed 260-day year is substituted.

The effective annual IRR discounts each payment using its actual calendar-day offset divided by 365. It is an annual compounded cash-flow illustration, not a state-law disclosure or a legally specified nominal APR.

sections.title: How does the holdback scenario work?
paragraphs: With eligible sales of 5,000 per remittance interval and a 10% holdback, the assumed remittance is 500. The 65,000 contract total is completed in 130 remittances.

At 2,500 sales per interval, the remittance is 250 and the count grows to 260. This changes the modeled duration and annual IRR without changing the factor-based total. Actual sales fluctuations or reconciliation can produce a different path.

sections.title: Why can the last remittance be smaller?
paragraphs: For a 1,000 advance with a 1.30 factor and 300 normal remittances, four remittances pay 1,200 and the last pays only 100. The schedule never collects more than the modeled contract total.

The worksheet retains internal precision; actual debit rounding, additional fees and early-payoff provisions must be read from the contract. Extremely high annual IRR is marked above the display range rather than shown as a real zero.

questions.question: Is a factor rate of 1.30 the same as 30% APR?
questions.answer: No. It sets a 30% markup on the gross advance in this model. Annualized cash-flow cost also depends on net funding, remittance timing and amount.

questions.question: Does a slower sales assumption reduce the contract total?
questions.answer: No. It lengthens the constant-sales scenario while the entered factor still determines the same remittance total. Actual contract reconciliation rules are outside the model.

questions.question: Are bank holidays skipped?
questions.answer: No. The weekday calendar skips Saturday and Sunday only. The first remittance is entered explicitly; a contract-specific calendar can differ.

meta.title: Backdoor Roth IRA Calculator: 2026: Worked Comparison
meta.heading: Backdoor Roth IRA Calculator: 2026: Worked Comparison
meta.description: A backdoor Roth conversion is not automatically tax-free
meta.breadcrumb: Backdoor Roth IRA and pro-rata basis
meta.cardIntro: A backdoor Roth conversion is not automatically tax-free. With $7,500 established nondeductible basis, $92,500 left in included IRAs at year end and $7,500 converted, the ordinary pool is $100,000. Only $562.50 of the conversion is nontaxable; $6,937.50 is taxable.

backdoor-roth-ira.intro: Use established nondeductible basis and aggregate the year’s included IRA amounts for one person. Conversion-only mode is a narrow ordinary case; full-year mode separately tracks other included distributions and 2026 contributions made in early 2027.
backdoor-roth-ira.answer: A backdoor Roth conversion is not automatically tax-free. With $7,500 established nondeductible basis, $92,500 left in included IRAs at year end and $7,500 converted, the ordinary pool is $100,000. Only $562.50 of the conversion is nontaxable; $6,937.50 is taxable.
backdoor-roth-ira.exampleNote: Original illustrations checked against independent 70-digit Decimal dated cash-flow and IRA-basis arithmetic. No competitor parity, professional certification or actual lender approval is claimed.

sections.title: Why does the whole included IRA pool matter?
paragraphs: The default illustration has 7,500 basis, 92,500 in included year-end IRA values and 7,500 converted. Adding the conversion back to the denominator gives 100,000, so the nontaxable fraction is 7.5%.
Apply that fraction to the 7,500 conversion: 562.50 is nontaxable and 6,937.50 taxable. The 24% assumed incremental rate gives a 1,665 conversion-tax illustration, not a full tax return.
sections.formula: Eligible basis = prior basis + current-year nondeductible contributions − following-year portion. Fraction = min(1, eligible basis / (year-end IRA values + included rollovers + other distributions + conversions)). Remaining basis = total basis − both nontaxable allocations.

sections.title: Which account values are aggregated?
paragraphs: Use the person’s included traditional IRA balances, including traditional SEP and traditional SIMPLE balances where applicable, at December 31. Do not isolate a new nondeductible-contribution account or combine spouses.

Do not add Roth or employer qualified-plan balances. Included outstanding IRA-to-IRA rollovers are a separate input and must not already be counted in the year-end value. This worksheet does not determine SIMPLE conversion eligibility or qualified-plan rollover eligibility.

sections.title: What if the contribution and conversion happen in different years?
paragraphs: A calendar-2026 conversion belongs to 2026 even when connected to a contribution for a different tax year. Conversion-only mode assumes the entered 2026 contributions were made by December 31 and there were no other included distributions.

Full-year mode includes eligible early-2027 contributions for 2026 in total basis, but subtracts them from the 2026 allocation numerator. That following-year portion remains in carryforward basis. A late contribution cannot simply be applied backward to erase a 2026 taxable conversion.

sections.title: Why separate other included distributions?
paragraphs: If there are other included distributions, they share the nontaxable fraction with conversions. With 7,500 basis, 82,500 year-end values, 7,500 conversions and 10,000 other included distributions, the pool is 100,000.

The conversion uses 562.50 basis and the other distribution uses 750. Total basis used is 1,312.50, leaving 6,187.50. Each amount is counted once. Special distributions, repayments and deduction-worksheet adjustments need separate IRS instructions.

sections.title: Which rules are deliberately outside the tool?
paragraphs: This is an ordinary basis-allocation worksheet based on the published final 2026 form. The currently linked narrative instructions are the 2025 edition for context; the tool does not substitute draft 2026 instructions for final guidance.

Contribution eligibility and deduction amounts must already be established. The tool does not compute MAGI limits, contribution caps, RMD eligibility, special repayments, inherited-IRA rules, early-distribution additional tax, Roth five-year withdrawals, mega-backdoor employer plans or complete tax filing. Choose the unsupported-case option when special adjustments apply.

questions.question: Can I convert only the after-tax money in a new IRA?
questions.answer: The ordinary allocation uses the individual’s aggregate included IRA pool, not an account label. A separate new IRA does not by itself isolate basis.

questions.question: Does the calculator decide how much I may contribute?
questions.answer: No. Enter a contribution amount already determined eligible and nondeductible. The tax rate is also your supplied incremental assumption, not a bracket calculation.

questions.question: Does leftover basis disappear after a conversion?
questions.answer: No. This worksheet subtracts basis used on the conversion and other included distributions once, retaining the unused total, including the following-year contribution portion.
